claims.text: The as-produced additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The as-produced alloy exhibits columnar grains.
The as-produced alloy contains residual stresses.
The as-produced alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
High-temperature degradation and catastrophic failure are governed by compromise of a protective oxide scale through differential elemental diffusion.
The protective scale consists primarily of Al2O3 and possibly TiO2.
In oxidizing environments, rapid aluminum oxidation initially forms a protective scale.
Subsequent nonuniform oxide growth and grain-boundary stress accumulation cause scale spallation and embrittlement.
Under reducing conditions, inadequate protective-scale formation permits internal oxidation and void formation.
Oxide-scale formation, integrity, and adhesion are governed primarily by the diffusion kinetics of aluminum and titanium.
Nonuniform oxide growth or inadequate oxide formation produces stress concentrations and grain-boundary weakening.
Stress concentrations and grain-boundary weakening lead to catastrophic mechanical failure.
Oxidizing atmospheres promote catastrophic failure through scale spallation.
Reducing atmospheres promote catastrophic failure through internal void formation.
Relative to an inert-atmosphere baseline, high-oxygen exposure initially produces a thicker oxide scale and later causes spallation and embrittlement.
Relative to an inert-atmosphere baseline, reducing exposure produces incomplete oxide protection, increased internal oxidation and void formation, and earlier mechanical failure.
At comparable temperatures, the inert-atmosphere control undergoes slower degradation and retains more robust mechanical performance.
The predicted governing behavior applies between 700 and 900 °C when oxygen partial pressure significantly deviates from inert conditions.
Outside the stated temperature and atmosphere boundaries, different degradation mechanisms may dominate.
